title: Study Abroad Report: Tulane University, Stanford University
paragraphs: I did a clerkship at Tulane University in the United States for 12 weeks from April, and at a laboratory at Stanford University for 4 weeks in March. Writing this report now, I recall many things, such as the exam study and preparations for going abroad, the friends I made in the United States and the irreplaceable experiences, and I already feel nostalgic.

[What did I want to do by going abroad in the future?] I want to be involved in neuroscience in the future. In this study abroad, I wanted to explore my future career plan and learn what I should acquire from now on, so I applied to study in the United States, said to be the one superpower. But rather than just being sent, I thought about "what I want to do by going abroad," and, in words I received from a person I respect, I decided to "create opportunities myself and make them opportunities to learn myself." This time I acted with the following in mind. (1) To observe and gather information on American medicine, clinical practice and basic research alike, and get hints for my future image. (2) To act proactively in the United States and broaden myself and my outlook. (3) To become able to build relationships in English.

[GI, Pulmonary: practical study] In the Tulane University clerkship I did GI, Pulmonary, Neurology and ER. In GI and Pulmonary, the residents and fellows taught me enthusiastically, and gradually I was entrusted with the first touch of patients and became able to state my own opinions. The education was practical, and I was able to learn medicine in ways such as, "This patient's test result will come out by tomorrow, so read this paper, think about how to interpret it and present tomorrow." In my studying for the national exam from now on, too, I would like to study with the clinical setting in mind.

[Neurology] In Neurology I was allowed to follow patients and do initial visits in the outpatient clinic. Going around with excellent local students was also stimulating. In both the clerkship and lectures I was often suddenly asked my opinion in front of everyone. Without preparation time, and with much vague knowledge, stating my opinion logically on the spot about the treatment plan for the patient in front of me was hard at first. But I was given many presentation assignments, and through doing them the knowledge, words and templates I could use increased. As a result, when asked on the spot for a differential diagnosis or treatment plan, I became used to stating my opinion in front of everyone. For example, when I was able to assess the prognosis of coma extemporaneously in front of everyone, based on a paper I had read before, I felt a great sense of accomplishment. In Neurology, with a sense of urgency that "if you don't give your opinion, it's taken as if you know nothing," I made sure to have my own opinion and speak up actively. Because I spoke up actively, I was invited to an attending's home, went out and played with friends, and built relationships, which are good memories. I was also able to obtain a letter of recommendation, which had been my goal.

[ER: division of labor, specialization] The experience here was shocking. New Orleans is one of the most dangerous cities in the United States and has many poor people. The hospital where I did my clerkship was a state hospital for people without insurance or with insurance for low-income people. When I was shown emergency medicine at Stanford University, I had been told that "the American ER is a mirror reflecting the community," and I saw a distorted side of unequal American society while also reaffirming the good aspects of Japanese medicine. What impressed me most in the clerkship was the case of a patient who had been stabbed twice, in the neck and the back, and was brought in in cardiac arrest. There are trauma-specialist attendings, and when a patient who meets certain conditions arrives, a trauma team is formed. When the call from the emergency services comes in, the trauma team gathers in the trauma room right beside the entrance, and more than a dozen staff handle the case, with roles and even standing positions decided for each: the ER resident, the surgical resident, the trauma attending, the nurse entering information and the assisting nurse. The patient arrived being resuscitated by a machine, and from there the speed was overwhelming. They immediately opened the chest and performed direct cardiac massage and cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and I was moved when I saw the heart start to move. Within barely ten minutes the patient was in the operating room. It was a moment in which I glimpsed the division of labor and specialization of American medicine.

[Clerkship and other: friends, culture] Excellent students gather at Tulane from all over the world, and being able to interact with such students was stimulating. In addition, I had created a community at the Nagoya University School of Medicine for interacting with international students, and I was able to deepen my friendship there with a friend from Tulane whom I had met in it, and I made friends whom I could call lifelong friends. Through the stories I heard in such exchanges and by touching their values, I also came into contact with the American climate that values "division of labor," "rationality," "efficiency," "competition," "generalization," "independence" and "building an organization that makes good use of people." At the same time I felt a difference from Japan, where "everyone being the same" seems to be considered a virtue. My friends were also attending business school and medical school at the same time, and rather than simply riding a rail, it was natural to think about their own career plans and to think for themselves about what was necessary and do it. In such things I sensed a spirit of independence, and I felt the inner strength of the United States in various aspects such as economics and politics.

[Clerkship and other: research] One of the things I wanted to do in the United States was to observe basic and clinical research. I was looked after for one month in the laboratory of Dr. 西野 at Stanford University, was allowed to visit the laboratories of Dr. 岡田 and Dr. 土井 at the University of Pittsburgh and Dr. 澤 at JHU, and was allowed to hear from Dr. 原田 and Dr. 金井 at the Mayo Clinic and Dr. 坂野 at MGH. I was helped by various people from Nagoya University and heard a lot from various Japanese researchers, and I think I was able to broaden my outlook and knowledge. I take this opportunity to thank them. Thank you very much. As for basic research, the connections between clinical and basic people are often deep, and I was impressed that there were many PhDs even in clinical research. I felt that this may be what leads to the industrialization of medicine. As for facilities too, for example Stanford University has several MRI scanners for large animals, and I was impressed by the facilities and protocols designed with FDA approval and clinical research in mind. But rather than the facilities being generally impressive, my impression was that funds are abundant, there is an environment where one can concentrate on research, and there is manpower from gathering excellent people from all over the world.

And as for clinical research, I also felt a big difference. The Core Facility for clinical research has departments in which people other than M.D.s support clinical research, such as statisticians (for example, helping with prospective designs), research coordinators (gathering patients and helping with various procedures), clinical trial nurses, and clinical services (for example, collecting the necessary data when one wants to do a retrospective study); at the Pittsburgh cancer center alone, nearly 50 people worked there. I was told that they support not only clinical trials but also so-called clinical research. In addition, what impressed me especially at the Mayo Clinic was that there is a practical database for clinical research that makes retrospective clinical studies easy. Such an environment makes it easier for ordinary doctors to choose clinical research over basic research when building a career, and in fact the students and fellows I was doing rounds with at Tulane said that in the next period they would do a retrospective clinical study based on the database. I felt that a climate in which each person thinks about and chooses their own career, and an environment that makes clinical research easy, may be one reason clinical research is so active in the United States. I was also impressed that at many universities epidemiologists, researchers and clinicians collaborate and one could feel an eagerness to create the first standard themselves.

[Japan in the world, as a physician] Studying abroad gave me an opportunity to look at life with a wide perspective. It is my personal view, but I think that globalization will advance further in the world and international economic competition will intensify, and that in this situation Japanese medicine will go in two major directions. One is the efficiency of medical care, and the other is the industrialization of medical care. Today, as the society of low birth rates and aging advances rapidly and the share of social insurance costs in tax revenue grows rapidly, it seems difficult to maintain universal health insurance in its present form. But politically the hurdle to abolishing universal health insurance is very high, and in this situation, in order to keep medical care going as "the same service at the same price for all citizens," I think that the "abolition of or strong restrictions on free access" and "the introduction of a more full-fledged family doctor system," which are common in Europe, will be the key. The introduction of a super-rotation emphasizing primary care and the recent debate around the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's creation of a general specialist also seem understandable from the viewpoint of aiming to train doctors who can do primary care and to guide medical care by making specialists easier to use through medical fee schedules. Regardless of how far it will actually go, I think the administration's goal is, in the end, as in the United States, to set strictly the quota for each hospital's residency program and to control the number of doctors in each department to some extent administratively.

And next, the industrialization of medical care. I think the policy of promoting industrialization of medical care does not differ much under any administration. For example, "industrialization of medical care" is included in the growth strategy, one of the three pillars of Abenomics, and the creation of a Japanese version of the NIH, which would enable budget allocation to promote cooperation among industry, government and academia and to make research efficient and industrial, is under consideration. Japan has world-class basic research and seeds, and promoting translational research seems to be a social demand. In the future I think PhDs will increase within medical schools, support systems for a wider range of clinical research than now will be created, and the clinical research environment toward industrialization will be developed, such as employing statisticians and people with know-how in drug discovery. On the other hand, at the individual level, I think it is common for physicians and researchers to build their careers within the framework of specialized clinical or basic departments.

[Toward the future] In the future I want to become a researcher and physician involved in neurons and glia. Among the various images of physicians and researchers, I think I was able to consider, based on my study abroad experience, what options might be possible for me. First, if industrialization as described above advances in Japan, I thought that MDs who know the clinical setting, have a foundation in clinical and basic research, and can connect basic and clinical through building relationships with various specialists will also be needed. At the same time, I want to aim to be a physician and researcher who values simple questions and curiosity. I hope to take on basic research eventually, but first I would like to take an interest in clinical research, even simple research, early on, listen to the talks of such specialists, and learn the groundwork. As for future study abroad, I learned that going abroad for clinical research is also an option. And when I feel the need to study abroad in the future, I felt that I want to research the destination well and, whether for basic or clinical research, acquire the survival spirit, English ability and communication skills to compete there rather than be treated as a guest.

[Support and gratitude] In this study abroad, I realized that I am supported by many people. I want to make this wonderful experience shine even more by making use of it in my life from now on. I thank the doctors I met at my destination, my fellow exchange students, my friends, the doctors and staff of the International Exchange Office, and my family. I thank everyone who supported my study abroad. Thank you very much.
